question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning given below?

To regard a statement with reservation; not to accept it as being wholly true.
option_1: To take with a pinch of salt
option_3: To rub salt into the wound
solution_text:
The correct answer is To take with a pinch of salt.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "to take something with a pinch of salt" means to treat a statement with scepticism, and not to believe the whole of it.

 

• Example: *His account of the meeting should be taken with a pinch of salt, since he was not present for most of it.*

 

• All four alternatives are genuine salt idioms with quite distinct meanings, so the answer must be settled on sense alone.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The American form is "with a grain of salt", a translation of the Latin cum grano salis. The phrase is traced to Pliny the Elder, who recorded an antidote to poison that was to be swallowed with a grain of salt — the salt making an unlikely remedy easier to accept.

 

NOTE

 

• To be worth one's salt (Option 2): To be competent and deserving of one's pay. The expression recalls the Roman *salarium*, the allowance given to soldiers to buy salt, from which the word salary descends.

 

• To rub salt into the wound (Option 3): To make an injury or humiliation worse by some further act. It concerns aggravating an injury, not doubting a statement.

 

• The salt of the earth (Option 4): A person of great worth, honesty and reliability. It is a term of high praise, and has nothing to do with scepticism.

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning given below?

To treat someone in a deliberately unfriendly and dismissive way; to ignore them pointedly.
option_1: To give someone the cold shoulder
option_3: To put one’s shoulder to the wheel
option_4: To have a chip on one’s shoulder
solution_text:
The correct answer is To give someone the cold shoulder.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "to give someone the cold shoulder" means to treat a person with deliberate coldness or indifference; to snub them.

 

• Example: *Ever since the dispute over the accounts, the whole department had given him the cold shoulder.*

 

• All four options are shoulder idioms, and each has a settled and quite separate meaning.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The related noun phrase is "a cold shoulder", and the verb is often used in the passive: *he was given the cold shoulder*.

 

• Idioms close in sense: to cut someone dead, to freeze someone out, to send someone to Coventry.

 

NOTE

 

• To rub shoulders with someone (Option 2): To mix socially with people, especially the famous or important. It denotes association, the very opposite of a snub.

 

• To put one's shoulder to the wheel (Option 3): To set to work with vigour and determination. It concerns effort, not attitude towards a person.

 

• To have a chip on one's shoulder (Option 4): To be resentful and easily provoked, usually because of a grievance one believes oneself to be nursing. Note that this describes the state of mind of the person himself, not his treatment of another.

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

To cut the Gordian knot.
option_1: To solve a long-standing and intricate problem by a single bold and decisive act
option_2: To untangle a dispute by patient negotiation carried on over a long period
option_3: To sever all connection with an old friend after a bitter quarrel
option_4: To make a difficulty worse by interfering in it clumsily
solution_text:
The correct answer is To solve a long-standing and intricate problem by a single bold and decisive act.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "to cut the Gordian knot" means to resolve a difficult and tangled problem by one swift, forceful and unconventional stroke, rather than by patiently working through it.

 

• Example: *Rather than argue the clauses one by one, the arbitrator cut the Gordian knot and cancelled the contract altogether.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The allusion is to a legend of Alexander the Great. At Gordium in Phrygia an intricate knot was tied to a chariot, and an oracle had promised the empire of Asia to whoever could untie it. Alexander, failing to loosen it by hand, drew his sword and cut it through.

 

• The point of the story, and of the idiom, is that the solution lay in refusing the terms of the problem rather than in greater patience.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 2 describes exactly what the idiom does not mean. Patient negotiation is the alternative that the bold stroke replaces.

 

• Option 3 takes the word *cut* literally and attaches it to a friendship. The nearer idiom for that sense is "to cut someone off".

 

• Option 4 describes clumsy interference, which is closer to the idea in "to muddy the waters". The Gordian stroke is decisive and successful, not bungling.

question: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bureaucracy.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct spelling is BUREAUCRACY, meaning a system of government or administration carried on by officials, or the body of such officials.

 

• The word is built from two parts, and each must be spelt correctly:

 

• BUREAU — the French word for a desk or office, spelt b-u-r-e-a-u. The commonest error is to begin it *beau-*, by confusion with the unrelated French word *beau* ("beautiful").

 

• -CRACY — from Greek kratos, "rule". Note that it is -cracy, never *-cacy*.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The -cracy family: democracy (rule by the people), autocracy (by one), aristocracy (by the best-born), plutocracy (by the wealthy), theocracy (by priests), meritocracy (by the able), kleptocracy (by thieves).

 

• Other words from *bureau*: bureaucrat, bureaucratic, and the plural bureaux or bureaus.

 

NOTE

 

• Beaurocracy (Option 1): Begins beau- instead of bure- — the classic confusion with *beau*.

 

• Bureacracy (Option 2): Gets *bure-* right but drops the u of *bureau*.

 

• Beauracracy (Option 4): Wrong at both points — the *beau-* opening, and a missing letter in the stem.

question: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Conscientious.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct spelling is CONSCIENTIOUS, meaning guided by one's sense of duty; careful and thorough in one's work.

 

• The word is best built from the noun it grows out of: conscience → conscienti- + -ous.

 

• The -sci- in the middle must be kept — it comes from Latin scire, "to know", the same root that gives science.

 

• The ending is -tious, not *-cious* — the t replaces the *ce* of *conscience*.

 

• The syllables run: con-sci-en-tious.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• A conscientious objector is one who refuses military service on grounds of conscience — a phrase in which both words come from the same root.

 

• Related words with the same sci element: conscience, conscious, omniscient, prescient, science.

 

NOTE

 

• Concientious (Option 1): Drops the s of *-sci-*, breaking the link with *conscience*.

 

• Conscientous (Option 2): Keeps the stem correctly but drops the i of the ending, giving *-tous* for *-tious*.

 

• Consciencious (Option 4): Retains the c of *conscience* where a t is required. This is the most tempting of the three errors, precisely because it looks closest to the parent word.

question:
Select the option with the correct spelling that can replace the underlined word in the given sentence. If the spelling in the given sentence is already correct, choose the option "No replacement required".

What had seemed an innocuous remark was seized upon by the opposition the following morning.
solution_text:
The correct answer is No replacement required.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The word "innocuous" is already spelt correctly in the sentence, so no replacement is needed.

 

• Innocuous means harmless; not likely to give offence or cause injury.

 

• The spelling to fix in memory is double N, single C: in-noc-u-ous. It comes from Latin in- ("not") + nocuus ("harmful"), from nocere, "to harm".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The same root nocere gives innocent (literally "not harming"), noxious (harmful), obnoxious and nuisance.

 

• Note the parallel pattern in innocent, innovate and innumerable — all take a double n because the prefix *in-* meets a stem beginning with *n*.

 

NOTE

 

• inocuous (Option 1): Single n — the prefix has not been doubled.

 

• innoccuous (Option 2): Correct double n, but an incorrect double c.

 

• inocuus (Option 3): The bare Latin form, not the English word.

 

• Remember that the "No replacement required" option is a genuine answer and not a last resort. In this question type, first test the given word letter by letter; only if it fails should you look at the three alternatives.

question:
Match the word with its closest synonym.

Word: Ubiquitous
solution_text:
The correct answer is Omnipresent.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ubiquitous (adjective) means present, appearing or found everywhere at the same time.

 

• Its closest synonym among the alternatives is Omnipresent, which means precisely the same thing.

 

• Example: *Within a decade the mobile telephone had become ubiquitous, from the largest city to the smallest village.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The two words reach the same meaning by different roads: ubiquitous from Latin ubique ("everywhere"), and omnipresent from omnis ("all") + praesens ("present").

 

• Other omni- words: omnipotent (all-powerful), omniscient (all-knowing), omnivorous (eating both plants and flesh).

 

NOTE

 

• Scarce (Option 2): Means insufficient in quantity; hard to find — the direct antonym of ubiquitous, and the principal trap here.

 

• Ambiguous (Option 3): Means open to more than one interpretation. It is included because it resembles *ubiquitous* in sound and ending, not in sense.

 

• Transient (Option 4): Means lasting only a short time. Note that it concerns time, whereas ubiquitous concerns place — a thing may be everywhere and yet brief.

question:
Choose the correct synonym for the underlined word in the given sentence.

The treaty was abrogated by the new government within a month of its taking office.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Annulled.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Abrogate (verb) means to repeal or formally do away with a law, agreement or custom.

 

• Its closest synonym among the alternatives is Annulled, which likewise means declared void and of no effect.

 

• Corrected reading: *The treaty was annulled by the new government within a month of its taking office.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other synonyms: repeal, revoke, rescind, nullify, abolish, cancel.

 

• Distinguish carefully between three words that look alike:

 

• Abrogate – to repeal or abolish (a law)

 

• Arrogate – to claim or seize something without right (*he arrogated to himself the powers of the board*)

 

• Abnegate – to renounce or give up (a right or pleasure)

 

NOTE

 

• Ratified (Option 1): Means formally approved and confirmed — the direct opposite of abrogated, and the trap in this question. A treaty is ratified when it is brought into force, abrogated when it is done away with.

 

• Amended (Option 2): Means altered in some particular. An amendment changes a document; abrogation destroys it altogether.

 

• Extended (Option 3): Means prolonged in time, which would keep the treaty alive rather than end it.

question: Choose the word that is most opposite in meaning to "ephemeral".
solution_text:
The correct answer is Everlasting.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ephemeral (adjective) means lasting for a very short time; short-lived.

 

• Its direct antonym is Everlasting, meaning lasting for ever or for a very long time.

 

• Example: *The fame of a season's cricketer is ephemeral; that of a Bradman is everlasting.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The word comes from Greek ephemeros, "lasting only a day". The mayfly, whose adult life is a matter of hours, belongs to the order Ephemeroptera — named from the same root.

 

• Other antonyms: permanent, perpetual, enduring, abiding, imperishable.

 

NOTE

 

• The question is built so that three of the four options are near-synonyms of the key word. Recognising that shape at once is faster than weighing each option in turn.

 

• Transitory (Option 1): Means not permanent; passing — a synonym.

 

• Fleeting (Option 2): Means passing swiftly — a second synonym.

 

• Momentary (Option 4): Means lasting only a moment — a third.

question: Choose the word that is the antonym of the phrasal verb "turn down".
solution_text:
The correct answer is Accept.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The phrasal verb "turn down" means to refuse or reject an offer, request or application.

 

• Its antonym is therefore Accept.

 

• Example: *He turned down the transfer twice before accepting it on the third offer.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• "Turn down" has a second sense — *to reduce the volume or intensity of something* (*turn down the radio*). Both senses are examined, and the options offered must decide which is meant. Here all four concern offers, so the first sense applies.

 

• Other phrasal verbs on turn:

 

• Turn up – arrive, often unexpectedly; or increase the volume

 

• Turn in – hand over; or go to bed

 

• Turn out – prove to be; or attend in numbers

 

• Turn over – hand across; or achieve a volume of business

 

• Turn on / turn against – attack suddenly / become hostile to

 

NOTE

 

• Reject (Option 1): Means to refuse to accept — a synonym of turn down, not its opposite.

 

• Refuse (Option 2): Means to say no to — a second synonym, and the plainest of the three.

 

• Decline (Option 4): Means to refuse politely — a third synonym. Note its unrelated second sense, *to decrease* (*a declining population*), which is not in question here.

question: Choose the word that is the antonym of the phrasal verb "call off".
solution_text:
The correct answer is Commence.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The phrasal verb "call off" means to cancel an event, or to abandon something already in progress.

 

• Its antonym is Commence, meaning to begin or start.

 

• Example: *The search was called off at dusk and recommenced at first light.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other phrasal verbs on call:

 

• Call on / call upon – pay a short visit; or formally request someone to speak

 

• Call for – demand or require (*the situation calls for patience*)

 

• Call up – summon for military service; or telephone

 

• Call in – summon for help (*call in a specialist*); or withdraw from circulation

 

• Call out – summon to action; or challenge publicly

 

NOTE

 

• Cancel (Option 1): Means to decide that a planned event will not take place — the plainest synonym of call off.

 

• Abandon (Option 2): Means to give up completely, and matches the second sense of call off, in which something already begun is discontinued.

 

• Scrap (Option 4): Means to discard a plan as useless — a third synonym, differing only in being more informal.

question:
Choose the most suitable one-word substitution for the following.

A person in charge of a museum or of a collection of works of art.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Curator.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A curator is the person in charge of a museum, gallery or collection — responsible for acquiring, cataloguing, conserving and displaying its objects.

 

• The word comes from Latin curare, "to take care of", the same root that gives cure and curator in its older legal sense of a guardian.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Keepers of things, distinguished:

 

• Curator – a museum or art collection

 

• Archivist – archives, that is historical records and documents

 

• Librarian – a library of books

 

• Custodian – a building or property, in the sense of a caretaker

 

• Registrar – an official register of records

 

NOTE

 

• Custodian (Option 2): One who has custody or care of a building or property — a caretaker or guardian. The word is broader and does not imply expertise in the collection itself.

 

• Archivist (Option 3): One who keeps and organises archives — historical documents and records rather than objects on display. This is the closest distractor.

 

• Connoisseur (Option 4): An expert judge in matters of taste, especially of art, food or wine. A connoisseur possesses discernment but holds no office and has charge of nothing.

question:
Choose the most suitable one-word substitution for the following.

A person who studies handwriting, especially in order to judge character or to determine authorship.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Graphologist.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A graphologist is one who studies handwriting, whether to infer the character of the writer or to establish who wrote a document.

 

• The word is formed from Greek graphein ("to write") + logos ("study of").

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The graphein family is a rich source of one-word substitutions:

 

• Calligrapher – one who practises beautiful handwriting

 

• Stenographer – one who writes in shorthand

 

• Cartographer – one who draws maps

 

• Choreographer – one who composes dance

 

• Biographer / Autobiographer – one who writes a life, of another or of himself

 

• Lexicographer – one who compiles dictionaries

 

NOTE

 

• Cryptographer (Option 1): One who works with codes and ciphers — from *kryptos*, "hidden". The concern is with concealing or deciphering a message, not with the hand that wrote it.

 

• Palaeographer (Option 2): One who studies ancient writing and manuscripts, in order to read and date them. This is the closest distractor: a palaeographer studies old scripts as historical evidence, whereas a graphologist studies handwriting for what it reveals of the writer.

 

• Stenographer (Option 4): One who writes in shorthand and transcribes dictation. The word denotes a skill in writing, not a study of it.

question:
Choose the most suitable one-word substitution for the following.

An introductory statement at the beginning of a book, written by the author, explaining its purpose and scope.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Preface.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A preface is an introductory statement at the beginning of a book, written by the author himself, in which he explains the purpose, scope and occasion of the work, and often records his acknowledgements.

 

• The decisive word in the definition is "by the author". That single condition separates a preface from a foreword.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The parts of a book, distinguished:

 

• Preface – introduction by the author

 

• Foreword – introduction by someone other than the author, usually a person of standing who commends the work

 

• Prologue – an opening section of a literary or dramatic work, forming part of the narrative itself

 

• Epilogue – a closing section of a narrative

 

• Postscript (P.S.) – an addition made after a letter or book has been finished

 

• Appendix – supplementary matter at the end; Glossary – explained terms; Bibliography – works consulted; Index – alphabetical list of topics with page numbers

 

NOTE

 

• Foreword (Option 1): The closest distractor, and the one that decides the question. A foreword is written by another person, not by the author, so it fails the terms of the definition.

 

• Postscript (Option 2): Comes at the end, not the beginning.

 

• Prologue (Option 3): Belongs to the work itself — a speech or scene opening a play, or an opening chapter of a novel. It is not a statement about the book's purpose.

question:
Select the correct alternative to fill in the blank with the correct preposition in the following sentence.

The new tariff policy was not conducive _____ the growth of small industry.
solution_text:
The correct answer is to.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The adjective conducive is always followed by the preposition to: *conducive to health, conducive to growth, conducive to learning*.

 

• Completed sentence: *The new tariff policy was not conducive to the growth of small industry.*

 

• Conducive means tending to bring about or make possible.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Adjectives that take "to" — a group worth learning as a block: *conducive to, averse to, partial to, prone to, liable to, susceptible to, indifferent to, sensitive to, akin to, hostile to, preferable to, inferior to, superior to, senior to, junior to*.

 

• Note especially that inferior, superior, senior, junior and preferable take to, never *than* — a very common error.

 

NOTE

 

• for (Option 1): The likeliest trap, since *good for growth* is idiomatic. But *conducive* has its own fixed preposition and does not follow the pattern of *good*.

 

• in (Option 3): Used with adjectives such as *deficient in, rich in, weak in, proficient in* — not with *conducive*.

 

• with (Option 4): Used with *consistent with, compatible with, familiar with, contented with* — again a different set.

question:
Select the correct alternative to fill in the blank with the correct preposition in the following sentence.

The senior clerk was conversant _____ every detail of the file.
solution_text:
The correct answer is with.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The adjective conversant is followed by the preposition with: *conversant with the rules, conversant with the facts*.

 

• Completed sentence: *The senior clerk was conversant with every detail of the file.*

 

• Conversant with means thoroughly acquainted with; having a good knowledge of.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Adjectives that take "with": *conversant with, acquainted with, familiar with, popular with, satisfied with, contented with, consistent with, compatible with, fraught with, replete with, busy with*.

 

• A useful contrast: one is acquainted with a subject but an expert in it; familiar with a rule but proficient in a skill.

 

NOTE

 

• in (Option 1): The strongest distractor, because *versed* — a word of similar sense — takes in (*well versed in the law*). *Conversant*, however, takes with.

 

• of (Option 2): Used with *aware of, capable of, guilty of, devoid of, desirous of, envious of* — not with *conversant*.

 

• about (Option 4): Used with *anxious about, curious about, particular about, doubtful about*. It would suggest merely having heard of the file, not knowing it thoroughly.

question:
In the given question, a sentence is divided into four parts and given in the alternatives 1, 2, 3 and 4. There is an error in one part. Choose the alternative containing that part of the sentence which has the error.

Neither the manager nor his assistants/ was present at the meeting/ that had been called/ to review the quarterly accounts.
option_1: Neither the manager nor his assistants
solution_text:
The correct answer is was present at the meeting.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The error lies in the agreement of the verb with the subject.

 

• When two subjects are joined by either...or or neither...nor, the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it — this is the rule of proximity.

 

• Here the nearer subject is "his assistants", which is plural. The verb must therefore be were, not *was*.

 

• Corrected sentence: *Neither the manager nor his assistants were present at the meeting that had been called to review the quarterly accounts.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Had the order of the subjects been reversed — *Neither the assistants nor the manager* — the nearer subject would be singular, and was would then be correct. Careful writers place the plural subject second for exactly this reason, since a plural verb sounds more natural.

 

• The rule of proximity governs either...or, neither...nor, not only...but also, and or standing alone.

 

• Contrast this with subjects joined by and, which take a plural verb, and with "as well as", "along with", "in addition to", "besides", "together with", which do not affect the number of the verb — the verb agrees with the first subject alone: *The manager, along with his assistants, was present.*

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 is correct. Neither...nor is the proper correlative pair; the error is not in the subject but in the verb that follows it.

 

• Option 3 is correct. "that had been called" is a properly formed relative clause in the past perfect passive, since the calling preceded the meeting.

 

• Option 4 is correct. The infinitive "to review" properly expresses the purpose for which the meeting had been called.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. The young clerk in the Calcutta office had been set to copy out the accounts of the season’s indigo.
A. He said nothing to anybody, but that night he copied the page a second time, and kept the second copy in his own trunk.
B. The sums were long, and for three days he copied them without once lifting his eyes from the page.
C. On the fourth day a figure caught his attention: one consignment had been entered twice, under two different dates.
D. He turned back to the ledger of the previous season, and found the same entry doubled there also.
S2. It was eleven months before anybody asked him a question about the indigo accounts, and by then he had six such pages in his trunk.
solution_text:
The correct answer is BCDA.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The paragraph is a narrative governed by a calendar, and the dates settle the order beyond dispute.

 

• B covers "three days" of unbroken copying, following naturally from S1, which tells us what he was set to do.

 

• C opens "On the fourth day", which must come after the three days of B. C introduces the discovery — a consignment entered twice.

 

• D follows C by investigation: having noticed one doubled entry, he turns back to the previous season's ledger and finds the same thing. D cannot precede C, since one does not verify a suspicion before forming it.

 

• A gives his response to what he has found — silence, and a private copy. It must come last of the four, because *"He said nothing"* presupposes that there is now something to say.

 

• S2 confirms the reading: eleven months later he has six such pages, which follows from the practice begun in A.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The governing sequence here is routine → interruption → verification → response, which is the standard shape of a discovery narrative. Identify that shape and the ordering follows.

 

NOTE

 

• DBAC (Option 2): Opens with D, so he checks the previous season's ledger before anything has aroused his suspicion.

 

• CDAB (Option 3): Opens with C, whose *"On the fourth day"* has no first three days to follow, and strands B at the end.

 

• BDCA (Option 4): Places D before C, reversing the discovery and its verification. This is the most tempting of the wrong options, since B and A are correctly placed at the ends.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. The letter reached Nirmala on a Tuesday, three weeks after it had been posted.
A. It was in her brother’s hand, though the writing wavered in a way she had never seen in it before.
B. She read it twice standing in the doorway, and a third time after she had sat down.
C. There was no address at the top of the sheet, and no date.
D. Only at the very end, below the signature, stood a single line she could not at first make out.
S2. When at last she deciphered it, she folded the letter away and did not speak of it to anybody for a month.
solution_text:
The correct answer is ABCD.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• All four options begin with A or C, and the first step is to see that A must open the sequence. S1 refers to the letter only as *"The letter"*; A supplies the first fact about it — *"It was in her brother's hand"* — and the pronoun "It" takes S1 as its antecedent.

 

• B follows: having recognised the hand, she reads it — twice standing, and a third time seated.

 

• C and D then examine the sheet itself, and their order is fixed by a plain contrast of position:

 

• C looks at "the top of the sheet" — no address, no date.

 

• D looks at "the very end, below the signature".

 

• A paragraph moves from the top of a page to its end, not the reverse, so C must precede D.

 

• S2 — *"When at last she deciphered it"* — refers to the line she *"could not at first make out"* in D, which confirms that D stands immediately before it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Two devices decided this question, and both recur constantly in para jumbles:

 

• A pronoun without an antecedent cannot open a sequence.

 

• Spatial markers — *at the top*, *below the signature*, *at the very end* — impose their own order, exactly as time markers do.

 

NOTE

 

• ACBD (Option 1): Separates C and D, so that the eye travels from the top of the sheet, away to the reading, and back to the foot of the page.

 

• ACDB (Option 2): Places B after D, so that she begins to read the letter only after she has already puzzled over its last line — and S2's *"When at last she deciphered it"* is left with nothing immediately before it to refer to.

 

• CABD (Option 3): Opens with C, describing a sheet that has not yet been identified as the letter of S1.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. The two clerks had shared the same room for eleven years and had never once quarrelled.
A. Sen took the desk by the window and Bose the one by the door, and neither had ever proposed an exchange.
B. Each knew to the minute when the other would rise to fetch a file, and moved aside without being asked.
C. They had settled the important questions early, and had never afterwards reopened them.
D. What they had never settled, and what neither of them could have explained, was why in eleven years they had spoken to each other of nothing but work.
S2. When the room was at last divided by a partition, both of them said that it made no difference whatever.
solution_text:
The correct answer is CABD.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• S1 makes the claim — eleven years, never a quarrel. The paragraph must explain how such peace was kept.

 

• C gives the explanation in general terms: *"They had settled the important questions early."* A general statement of this kind is naturally followed by an instance.

 

• A supplies exactly that instance — the division of the desks, settled once and never reopened. A therefore follows C.

 

• B carries the same idea further, from a settled arrangement to an unspoken daily habit: each knew when the other would rise, and moved aside unasked. It shows the understanding operating from minute to minute.

 

• D must come last of the four. It opens "What they had never settled", which turns directly on the *"settled"* of C, and it delivers the reservation the whole portrait has been building towards — that in eleven years they had spoken of nothing but work.

 

• S2 completes the point: a partition between them made no difference whatever.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The paragraph follows the pattern general statement → particular instance → further instance → the reservation that gives the portrait its point. Where a paragraph ends on a reservation, the sentence carrying it is almost always the last of the jumbled four.

 

NOTE

 

• CBDA (Option 1): Places D before A, so the reservation is delivered and the paragraph then returns to the seating arrangement — an anticlimax, and it breaks the link between D and S2.

 

• ACDB (Option 2): Opens with the instance A before the general statement C that explains it, and ends with B, leaving D stranded in the middle.

 

• DCAB (Option 4): Opens with D, whose *"What they had never settled"* refers back to a *settling* that has not yet been mentioned.

Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions based on the passage:

 

The idea of human rights is commonly set out in three generations, a scheme proposed by the jurist Karel Vasak, each generation answering to the conditions and the anxieties of the period that produced it. The first generation consists of civil and political rights — freedom of speech, freedom from arbitrary arrest, the right to a fair trial and the right to vote. These are sometimes called negative rights, because what they principally require of the state is that it should refrain from acting; their classic statement is found in the revolutionary declarations of the eighteenth century. The second generation consists of economic, social and cultural rights — to work, to education, to health and to social security. These are positive rights, for they oblige the state to act and to spend, and they entered international law chiefly through the covenant of 1966 and through the constitutions written after the Second World War. The third generation, of which Vasak himself was the principal advocate, consists of rights held not by individuals but by peoples in common — to development, to a healthy environment, to peace, and to a share in the common heritage of mankind. Critics of this third generation have argued that a right belonging to everyone in general belongs to no one in particular, and that a right without an identifiable holder and an identifiable duty-bearer cannot be enforced at all. Its defenders reply that the same objection was raised, in its own day, against each of the two generations that came before.

 

What was the principal concern of the first generation of rights?
option_1: Civil and political rights, such as free speech and the right to vote
option_2: Economic and social rights, such as work, education and health
option_3: Rights held by peoples in common, such as development and peace
option_4: The enforcement of rights through international courts
solution_text:
The correct answer is Civil and political rights, such as free speech and the right to vote.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage states it directly: *"The first generation consists of civil and political rights — freedom of speech, freedom from arbitrary arrest, the right to a fair trial and the right to vote."*

 

• It adds that these are called negative rights, because what they chiefly demand of the state is that it should refrain from acting, and that their classic statement is found in the revolutionary declarations of the eighteenth century.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The word "negative" here carries no note of disapproval. It is a technical description: the duty imposed on the state is a duty of abstention — not to censor, not to arrest arbitrarily, not to deny a hearing.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 2 describes the second generation, which the passage assigns to a later period and a different kind of duty.

 

• Option 3 describes the third generation, of which Vasak himself was the principal advocate.

 

• Option 4 raises enforcement, which the passage discusses only in connection with the criticism of the third generation — not as the concern of the first.

question: दिल्ली सल्तनत के अंतिम वंश लोदी वंश की स्थापना किस वर्ष हुई थी?
solution_text:
सही उत्तर 1451 है।

 

महत्वपूर्ण बिंदु

 

• लोदी वंश की स्थापना 1451 में बहलोल लोदी ने की थी, जिसने अंतिम सैयद शासक आलम शाह को अपदस्थ कर दिया था। (लोदी वंश — 1451)

 

• यह दिल्ली सल्तनत का पाँचवाँ एवं अंतिम वंश था तथा दिल्ली पर शासन करने वाला पहला अफगान (पश्तून) वंश — इससे पूर्व के चारों वंश तुर्की अथवा सैयद वंशज थे।

 

• इसके तीन शासक थे — बहलोल लोदी (1451-89), सिकंदर लोदी (1489-1517) तथा इब्राहिम लोदी (1517-26)।

 

• इस वंश तथा सल्तनत दोनों का अंत 21 अप्रैल 1526 को पानीपत के प्रथम युद्ध में हुआ, जहाँ बाबर ने इब्राहिम लोदी को पराजित कर मार डाला।

 

अतः सही उत्तर विकल्प 1 है।

 

अतिरिक्त जानकारी

 

• दिल्ली सल्तनत के पाँच वंश:

 

• गुलाम / मामलूक – 1206-1290 (कुतुबुद्दीन ऐबक, इल्तुतमिश, रजिया, बलबन)

 

• खिलजी – 1290-1320 (जलालुद्दीन, अलाउद्दीन खिलजी)

 

• तुगलक – 1320-1414 (गयासुद्दीन, मुहम्मद बिन तुगलक, फिरोज शाह)

 

• सैयद – 1414-1451 (खिज्र खान)

 

• लोदी – 1451-1526

 

• सिकंदर लोदी ने 1504 में आगरा नगर की स्थापना की और अपनी राजधानी वहाँ स्थानांतरित की। इब्राहिम लोदी दिल्ली का एकमात्र सुल्तान है जिसकी मृत्यु युद्धभूमि में हुई।

 

नोट

 

• 1414 (विकल्प 2): इसी वर्ष खिज्र खान ने सैयद वंश की स्थापना की थी, जो तैमूर के अधीन पूर्व सूबेदार था — यही वह वंश था जिसे लोदियों ने अपदस्थ किया।

 

• 1489 (विकल्प 3): इसी वर्ष इस वंश का दूसरा एवं सर्वाधिक योग्य शासक सिकंदर लोदी सिंहासन पर बैठा।

 

• 1517 (विकल्प 4): इसी वर्ष इस वंश का अंतिम शासक इब्राहिम लोदी सिकंदर का उत्तराधिकारी बना।

question: दिल्ली सल्तनत के प्रशासन में नकद वेतन के स्थान पर किसी अधिकारी को दी जाने वाली वह भूमि, जिससे वह स्वयं राजस्व वसूल करता था, _____ कहलाती थी।
solution_text:
सही उत्तर इक्ता है।

 

महत्वपूर्ण बिंदु

 

• इक्ता किसी अमीर अथवा सैन्य अधिकारी को नकद वेतन के बदले दिया जाने वाला राजस्व निर्धारण था। इसका धारक, जिसे इक्तादार अथवा मुक्ती कहा जाता था, निर्धारित क्षेत्र का राजस्व वसूल करता, उसी में से अपना वेतन रखता, उसी से सैनिकों की टुकड़ी रखता तथा शेष राशि राजकोष में भेज देता था। (इक्ता व्यवस्था)

 

• भारत में यह व्यवस्था इल्तुतमिश ने आरंभ की थी, और यह सल्तनत के प्रशासन की रीढ़ थी।

 

• इक्ता हस्तांतरणीय होती थी, वंशानुगत नहीं — धारक को एक क्षेत्र से दूसरे क्षेत्र में बदल दिया जाता था ताकि वह स्थानीय शक्ति आधार न बना सके। बाद में फिरोज शाह तुगलक ने इन्हें वंशानुगत बना दिया, जिससे केंद्रीय सत्ता कमजोर हुई।

 

• अलाउद्दीन खिलजी ने अनेक इक्ताओं को पुनः प्रत्यक्ष नियंत्रण में लिया और अपने सैनिकों को नकद वेतन दिया।

 

अतः सही उत्तर विकल्प 2 है।

 

अतिरिक्त जानकारी

 

• सल्तनतकालीन प्रशासन के अन्य जानने योग्य शब्द:

 

• दीवान-ए-विजारत – वित्त; दीवान-ए-अर्ज – सैन्य विभाग, जिसकी स्थापना बलबन ने की

 

• दीवान-ए-रिसालत – धार्मिक मामले; दीवान-ए-इंशा – पत्राचार

 

• दीवान-ए-कोही – कृषि, जिसका गठन मुहम्मद बिन तुगलक ने किया

 

• दीवान-ए-खैरात – दान, तथा दीवान-ए-बंदगान – दास, दोनों का गठन फिरोज शाह तुगलक ने किया

 

नोट

 

• खालिसा (विकल्प 1): सीधे राजमुकुट के अधीन भूमि, जिसका राजस्व किसी बिचौलिए के बिना सीधे राजकोष में जाता था।

 

• इनाम (विकल्प 3): राजस्व-मुक्त अनुदान, जो प्रायः विद्वानों, धर्मपरायण व्यक्तियों अथवा राजकीय कृपापात्रों को दिया जाता था। इस पर सैनिक रखने का कोई दायित्व नहीं होता था।

 

• वक्फ (विकल्प 4): इस्लामी विधि के अंतर्गत धार्मिक बंदोबस्ती, जिसमें संपत्ति सदा के लिए किसी धर्मार्थ अथवा पुण्य कार्य को समर्पित कर दी जाती है और उसके बाद उसे न बेचा जा सकता है और न ही वह उत्तराधिकार में जाती है।
